why: Both moved the single call identically and honestly, but A's system-level read is deeper and better ranked for this specific app — it names the real cost driver (the whole reply chain resent every turn with a clock destroying the cacheable prefix), ships the three levers an interactive bot most needs (cache key, cross-vendor fallback, 60s provider_timeout), and backs them with a harness that actually drives on_message rather than importing it. B lands the sharpest single idea A missed — an opt-in `router` provider that puts the whole catalog in the /model picker, live-verified across anthropic and fireworks — plus a genuine per-message client/connection-pool leak fix and a better per-channel cache key, but its remaining judgment is thinner (no token-vs-character budget, no per-guild spend labels, no model-price analysis, no Responses-native end state).
A_best: The improvement set reads the app rather than the API: it identifies that llmcord's economics are 'resend the full chain every turn', fixes the clock-first prompt that made caching impossible, and then ranks beyond it — char-based chain caps replaced by Router's free count_tokens, per-guild/user metadata for chargeback, cheaper-default price multiples, and per-channel model selection as the rework it would do first.
B_best: i1: adding Router as a config provider with api.router.com unlocked, so the bot's entire UX (a model picker) reaches Claude/Grok/DeepSeek on one key with no new provider block — opt-in, default model unchanged, and proven live on two non-OpenAI vendors.
A_worst: Each improvement branch writes its own single-key router.policy.json, so the three levers collide if combined (acknowledged only in passing), and the cache key is the static `$feature` for every channel and user, which is a weaker choice than per-conversation; it also calls m1/s1 losses 'nothing' while non-Router providers plainly stay outside Router's spend view.
B_worst: Fallback, provider_timeout and user-visible failure reporting are all left as unbuilt proposals, so the reliability half of the migration ships as text; the one shipped non-Router change (client reuse) is good engineering but unrelated to Router leverage, and no claim about this app's cache behaviour was measured.
